reviews.review: Too buggy and poorly implemented to want to push through the steep learning curve. The main thing that offends me as a programmer: busted error messages. Type in the right command but the wrong web address, and it tells you "command not found". Give the wrong file as evidence, and you get a message that implies you got the location wrong instead. etc. I'm glad I didn't pay much for this but I don't think it's worth it, even at a steep discount.

I feel like I overpaid. This has the makings of a decent game, but is soooooo glitchy. I kept having to restart the cases to fix the glitches. I should not have to do that multiple times in a game you can complete in one siting. Also, it was pretty short. Wait until the game is at least 50% off. $16 was way too much to pay for this game. I wish the developer had gone back over the game, but clearly they have no intention of doing so. I'd love to see a similar game by a better developer. If it's cheap enough, go ahead and get it. It was enjoyable enough to recommend at the right price.
It is really fun, anyone would like it

This game is short but sweet, very very sweet, it had a feel similar to Orwell except for the fact that it doesn't highlight clues for you, it was both challenging and easy to grasp and get into and not want to leave. I did find the story overall pretty good and I can't wait to see future projects from these developers. 
The one downside for this game is replay value where it sits with little to none, but for me that is not too bad.
In summary if you like espionage/ surveillance games (such as Orwell, Don't Feed The Monkeys, etc.,) what are you waiting for this game is Awesome!!

Great story-line, interesting puzzles, different outcomes for each level is an amazing feature; you must really use your brain to be able to crack all of them.
I finished the game in a little over 4 hours and I got the game with a discount (85% off) during the summer sale, so I'd say it was 100% worth it. Maybe 12.49 euros (the full price for the Deluxe edition) is a little more than I'd be willing to pay for a 5-hours game.

Suggestions:
   -I believe we should be able to make multiple arrests/level, if there are multiple suspects
   -I had a difficult time typing, because, in case of a typo, you can't move through the text using the arrows/mouse; you have to delete everything up to the point at which you want to edit the text. 
   -An award-system would be a great addition! (like Steam achievements)
needed a tutorial for every level lets go

The concept seemed neat, and I had a decent time playing it. The story was also mostly interesting to me... seems like all the makings of a great game! Unfortunately, the countless technical issues and glitches I've encountered (issues with things not taking input/dropping keys/having to reload the level) are annoying, and it seems like there may be some slight hiccups in some ingame text grammatically/some placeholders that slightly ruin the immersion. From some Steam discussion board threads I saw it seems like the dev is no longer supporting the game, so it looks like some of those bugs will never be fixed. These annoyances and glitches make this a not recommended for me. :(

Such an amazing story and so many approaches to implement in order to solve crimes! This game really challenges your skills to look for answers and retrieve data out of everything within your line of sight. The design is simply tremendous, such endeavours were put into making the operating systems look authentic that you couldn't help but forget you're in the game.

The game threw me some heckin side curves but in the end it was really fun! Would not recommend the full price, but if it's on sale I highly recommend it! Side note: the story's so good, I'd pay a whole movie theater ticket for a movie adaption.
Recommended if you prefer good stories in games, not recommended if you prefer having noticeably different results based off your choices.
crashes too much however that sprobaly my computer fault and in the time i was playing it the game wasn't bad
Yes.

I loved the idea of an interface-em'-up, and I'm going to keep plinking away at it later, but I just don't seem to like this game so far.  
     I know it's part of the aesthetic, but nothing fits on your monitor, leading to frustrating moments dragging things around to make enough space without closing something, as most of your screens cannot be resized or minimized. Additionally, sometimes when I had more than 2 windows open two of them would begin flickering wildly for some reason. Could chalk it up to intentional jank because of the old-style OS but it sure looked like a bug to me.
     Beyond that, there's a lot of weird things that have been left out in terms of usability: you cannot use the arrow keys to go back on a line of text, so you have to delete and retype if you make an error. Nor can you use the up key to go to a previously entered line of code in the command-line more than once.
    What this leads to is enough irritation in the first two cases (suppose I should have played the demo) that I am already going to set the game down until I have the patience to give it another shot, at which point if I can hack it through I'll update this review.
    I will say that the atmosphere provided is pretty nice. The gentle music in the background with the sounds of the street outside, combined with the hilariously exaggerated typing and clicking sounds that the game makes when you do those actions, well, it's kinda relaxing. There was a bit in case 2 where the music ramped up a bit, but it was while you're supposed to be watching someone drive around on google maps, and you have no agency, so I don't think it had the impact they were going for. Not on me anyhow.

I really adored this game!  Some hacker games have too high of learning curves, but this one had the perfect amount of action alongside the text. I've been sitting on this game in my inventory forever, and I'm SO glad I got to it. I took breaks to eat and sleep, but otherwise I was GLUED to my screen. There were a few puzzles that were tricky, but the internet gave me enough hints to get through without any complete walkthroughs.
This game is so much fun! The pixel graphics mixed with a cool concept and atmospheric music drew me in instantly. It's a great puzzle game that puts you in the mindset of a cybercop. 9/10

Very good game! loved the story line and playing detective while hacking.
I hope Mainlining could continue as a story and have a sequel.

I truly wanted to recommend this game because it has got so many things nicely done. Cute pixel art and simulated websites, dialogues between agents, decent story, amusing chat logs, good writing, moving from one clue to another, arresting someone each day... It isn't exactly a hacking simulation but that it isn't a big issue for me either. I played a lot of hacking simulation games and when I realized this isn't exactly one of them (hacking in this is all about typing only a handful console commands) I didn't care much, doing some simple detective work and enjoying it as if a visual novel could also be enough for me. 

Firstly, the game is a little buggy and sometimes crashes, I think it crashed 4 times during my playthrough, so I had to start a case from scratch while almost at the point of moving next one, because game autosaves only at the start of a new case. 

The real annoying problem with this game is the 'evidence' part. It is pretty simple. You download a lot of files, find the real names of the devious anti-government hackers who all have nicknames, then find really incriminating documents about them, then you attempt to arrest them using the very obvious document you have seized... but it doesn't work. The game says, with a newspaper article after your attempted to arrest, that the security service you work for has wrongly accused an innocent person. The document, although even the most incriminating one, blatantly mentioning everything about the hacker, his real name and activities is somehow the wrong document... Instead, it is one of the other documents with containing a lot less information, sometimes even not containing any information related to the case. So after awhile you give up, get extremely bored and simply go from file to file, trying each one of them to arrest the suspect and one of them works because devs decided only one of them should work even though there is not a concrete reason why only that one should work. I finished the game, but it was a througly annoying experience. I don't think I could have finished it if the game didn't have such good writing and story.

There are much better hacking simulation games out there, even if you have played all of them, I still recommend skipping this one because it doesn't award the time you spent on going through all those documents. Really badly designed, I don't what they were thinking.
Great, ambitious game that is only flawed by it's difficulty in controls, would benefit from shortcuts and scroll buttons.
Interesting concept, but poorly implemented. The arrest mechanism is...not good. It gets slightly more interesting later in the game, but then it's over.

Notwithstanding the occasional slight illogicalness and the counter-intuitiveness of the game mechanics and the slightly annoying bugs that happen ever so often, it's a game with a decent story that is worth playing, albeit perhaps only if purchased at a discounted price solely because of the mentioned flaws.

In the midst of an obsession with hacking sim games, Mainlining was a fun little departure from the "sim" type of game as it throws you into a fun little world with pretty clear-cut ways of "hacking".  The gameplay is pretty fun but the story is very short.  I completed this game in one sitting and felt disappointed that there wasn't more to it.  

I would recommend buying it on sale because there is little to no replay value.

According to Steam I've played this game for 6 hours. In none of that time did I feel like I was having fun and so at this point I feel it's a safe bet that the game never picks up. It all just feels like busy work. Also none of it resembles real hacking but, to be fair, I've never seen that properly captured in any game. The closest game to it that I've found is Else Heart.Break(), so go play that game instead!

The premise of being a dystopian cyber police officer is cool, but the evidence mechanic is very unintuitive at times. What makes sense as ideal evidence to prove someone guilty to you may be completely different from what the game developers had in mind. The fourth case was so bad I stopped playing. I would refund this game, but it's too cheap.

[spoiler] In the 4th case, you find a chat log of someone talking about planning a drug trade with somebody at a university. On the suspect's computer, there's a map of the university with a big, red circle marking the location of the trade deal. With this, one would think that the best evidence to convict the suspect of trading illegal substances would be the chat log, but nope, this game thought the map of the school was the proper evidence. How the hell is a university blueprint map with a red circle on it enough evidence to send someone to prison for 25 years?!? This is just one of many other logical issues that this game's evidence system has. [/spoiler]
This game is so creative! Really enjoy the hacking aspect and Ioving the storyline as well.

Very fun and engaging, and I've played through it at least twice. A must play if you like hacking games. I would love a sequel or more games with this format and design. Only downside is some of the episodes are a little shallow and short. I would have liked to go deeper into the story and have more stuff to do with the techs given. fairly easy puzzle game with an intuitive interface/game design. experienced a few glitches here and there (especially when switching windows via alt+tab) but overall it was a fun game. if you like puzzle games and have a few hours to kill... you should DEFINITELY give this game a try. :)

This game seems really good. I love all the writing and the game is engaging so far. However, it seems like saving the game doesn't work at all. The game is supposed to have an autosave feature (and you cannot manually save your progress), but the autosave never initiates.

You must play this entire game in 1 sitting. I recommend picking up this game when the game has been patched and autosaving works.

Fun puzzle  game with short cases to investigate.  You play as a federal agent hacking into civilian computers looking for evidence of crimes. The game has pretty simple mechanics that build with new applications and software to investigate over time.  The game doesn't hold your hand, often it doesn't even tell you which criminal to go after.  You can find evidence to put people away for 5, 10, or 25 years, so there is often multiple ways to approach an investigation with some harder than others.  Each case is short enough that you can do one or two if you only have a little bit of time to play.  I like a challenging puzzle game with simple to learn mechanics and enough of a story to motivate me to get to the next challenge.  That being said, the story isn't exactly "gripping".  There's enough story to keep the hacking and investigating from seeming pointless, but none of the characters are fleshed out much, there are no exciting twists, and the humor is hit or miss.  I didn't find any bugs.  Gameplay was solid.

Look, I'm sorry. This "gripping narrative" is inferior to Hacknet/Uplink/Hypnospace Outlaw/Insert Desktop Simulator Here in every single possible way. The fact that missions are bite sized and don't really tie together terribly well doesn't help, and it's horribly obtuse in terms of "puzzles" which are best summarized as downloading everything and attempting to use brute force to incriminate the target of the mission, because the file you think would work never does.

The characters are generic and uninteresting. The setting is generic and uninteresting. The web pages are generic and uninteresting. The console is generic and uninteresting. The interactions are generic and uninteresting. I could go on. I didn't think it was possible to fail at constructing a narrative this badly and still have people eat it up and leave positively glowing reviews.

There are better games to play if it's this genre. I can't actually recommend this in good faith, since it's just...not that good. It's like a Michael Bay film, except that this version of Michael Bay makes badly animated explosions that will only keep your attention if you've never seen a better explosion.

Let me start with a pro/con list so you don't have to sift through my personal thoughts in longform.

Pros:
-Doesn't hold your hand, feels 'authentic'. You feel like you're hacking, in some small way.
-Satisfying UI, easy to navigate without tutorial.
-Challenging without being mind-bendingly difficult or frustrating (usually).
-Interesting story with fun twists and turns and a lot of personal flourish to make it feel alive.
-Offers several solutions to almost every case, the result is up to what you turn in.
-Good music and ambient sound.
Cons:
-Bit of a buggy mess sometimes. Had to reset several cases when things stopped working, and had the entire game freeze at one point.
-Doesn't do much to make you feel "involved" in the story...you are a silent and non-engaging protagonist. Things happen to you and around you, you do not really interact except hacking.
-A few times, it suffers from "Figure out what the devs were thinking" syndrome.
-Lots of typos and a few places where things were not implemented but were left in the script for players to see

Mainlining is a good game with a lot of potential. I love the concept of an adventure game told through hacking and desktop UIs. But it really needs a good strong polish to truly be a satisfying experience. It's a short, light-hearted bit of fun, which I enjoyed! Don't expect a deep hacking experience like Uplink...this is primarily an adventure game. However, the narrative was too short and not engaging enough for me to really feel totally sucked in or invested....exciting things lose their emphasis because it's all told to you the same way with very little pause for breath or impact, or it happens "off screen".

However, I think this game is fun, interesting, unique and worth a play for sure. I found it easy to forgive its little hiccups and lack of polish because I was so charmed by Mainlining. If you enjoy feeling like a hacker, government intrigue, solving mysteries and adventure games, I think you will really find something to like here.

An interesting, yet cliche plot drives you through about three hours of missions as a member of a government intelligence agency. You need to put together information that isn't necessarily spoon fed to you to build a case. Determining what qualifies as sufficient evidence can be a little frustrating, but they thankfully keep the number of red herrings to a minimum. It's much more entertaining if you can go full screen and suspend reality a bit while you use their tools to crack the case. Definitely worth checking out, but do keep in mind that it might take four hours or less to get through the game and there is no replay value.

This was pretty fun for awhile.  I probably would've played it to the end if I had felt like the solutions to the cases were more clear.  I don't want to be spoon-fed or led by the nose, but even once I knew what the solution was to some of the cases, I still didn't understand why, based on the evidence. That seems to be a common complaint, and it's really too bad.  I still got enjoyment from the game, though, and maybe I'll give it another go sometime, so I still recommend it.

[b]/STORY and CHARACTERS (6/10)/[/b]

First things first, let's start with the story and characters. You're an agent from the government cyber security agency MI7 that investigates with other MI7 agents a group of hackers called Thorn who breached their servers. Your job is to track down all the members of the group and arrest them for a different crime in order to hide the security breach to the public. Alright, sounds simple enough, but that's because it IS simple, it's not more fleshed out than that. You spend the whole game hunting down an entire hacker group, then find an excuse to arrest them (I'll get back on that later). Even when you detain the big leader, none of what you've done felt satisfying after that.

As for the characters, well you don't have that much of character development from them, except for the "smart girl of the team" agent Sharp, the "bossy boss who takes his job way too seriously" Osvalt, the "I prefer old TTS softwares" agent on the field Cooper, the "flirty secretary who puts winky emojis all over her emails" Ashley, the "hahaha, I'm evil" hacker group leader Mr. Blue. Anyway, you get the point. Each character is only limited to one main characteristic and that's it.

[b]/GAMEPLAY (4/10)/[/b]

Oh boy, the gameplay is the main(lining) reason why I'm not recommending this. Jeez, where do I start? Well, first of all, if you're expecting to feel like a hacker, you're in for a disappointment. All you get is a command-prompt application with two script-kiddie commands: one that gets a website's IP and one that hacks into someone's computer using the said IP. That's right, throughout the whole game you'll spend most of your time typing 'ping', 'iphack', 'ping', 'iphack' while searching a computer's files in a DOS-style file navigation system. The devs claimed that it was on purpose in order to emphasize the narration over actual hacking. I would be fine with that kind of decision, but that doesn't mean you should stick to that repetitive "look at a website, ping, iphack and read files" bulls hit. At least keep an enjoyable gameplay in the background as well. Luckily, you get some other apps (like the google map one) and Operating Systems on the way.

On top of that, the arrest system is really nitpicky about which evidence you use against the person. Each case has around three alternate crimes to choose from to arrest the person you're tracking. However, only 1 evidence per crime is accepted code-wise. In other words, if you choose a proof that totally makes sense but wasn't chosen by the devs, it doesn't count. I ended up spamming the "begin arrest" button with every file I snatched.

As for the OS interfaces, it's a buggy mess, no matter which one is it. You start off with a parody Windows XP, which is pretty nice. You also get parody Ubuntu, parody Mac and parody Windows Vista/7 on the way, which is also great. The pixel art is pretty good, but the Operating Systems look so limited in comparison to the real thing, they don't feel like Operating Systems that anyone would actually use in real life (I know it's just a game, but come on). You can't delete files in your folder (too bad if you accidentally downloaded the same thing twice!) and the notepad doesn't save what you wrote into a text file, which is pretty inconvenient when I constantly need to write down IPs and names (and if you accidentally closed the notepad, too bad!). Also, if you keep windows open in Windows XP, then switch to another OS, open windows in that said OS, then switch back to Windows XP, the windows will start overlapping. I'm not impressed, man. Don't you have a "visible/invisible" property on your images or something in the engine you're using? Oh, and you're gonna love this one: the program is so delayed that if you type something way too fast, some keys will be ignored. Most of the time, you're going to have a lot of "mainlining" ending up like "manliin" because the game couldn't keep track of everything you typed down. This is super annoying when you type an IP, but get an error because the fucking game missed a keystroke and you don't know why it doesn't work since the error message doesn't tell you anything about what went wrong.

There are even reports of people who couldn't advance in some cases because the program forgot to add certain chat messages on the left to let you continue, which is frustrating when you can't even save in the middle of a case and instead start the whole thing over again. Luckily, I didn't encounter those case advancement bugs, but if you can't make a OS interface themed game with basic typing and windows manipulation without being overflowed with bugs, you shouldn't even sell it at 8-10 bucks. Personally, from my experience with this game, I think it should be five dollars at best, or even free.

[b]/CONCLUSION/[/b]

To conclude, I don't recommend this game. It's half-baked, it looks like a prototype game and doesn't have any satisfaction upon playing it whatsoever. The replayability value is somewhat there, but I put the game aside about two or three times before finally finishing it. If you feel like buying a hacking game without caring about anything else, then go for it. Otherwise, I'm giving this game...

[h1]5/10[/h1]
A very interesting game that makes you think.

This is a pretty well-done implementation of a cool idea.  You're on a Windows 95-analogue machine, trying to track down criminals with a very limited interface.  Come for the nostalgic dial tone, stay for the detective work of following down leads.

I had this game in my library for a while because I know it's the kind of game you really need to sit down and pay attention to. Finally got around to playing it, and in about 2 or so hours I got up to Case [Level] 4 in the game. It reminded me of "whodunnit" game (for example, Clue), where you find clues and apprehend a suspect. Except it's set entirely in a customized operating system where you can utilize the limited internet, email, command box, etc., to "hack" around and solve mysteries. 

I've always loved mystery games so I really like this game. It does require a bit of concentration and problem-solving, so it's probably not a game to play casually in the background while multitasking. There are little to no walkthroughs online, as it is a relatively indie game, so you have to be resourceful. That being said, it really isn't that difficult to get the hang of if you get creative.

Unlike some other "hacking" games I've played, this game is easier to pay attention to. First of all, Mainlining has a cartoonish, 8-bit style that makes it fun to look at. Second, other hacking games can sometimes be a bit more difficult as they more accurately depict coding, which makes it less fun if you don't have programming knowledge. This game is definitely more entertaining for casual gameplay.

I definitely plan on playing this game more in the future. I recommend it if you want to get into "hacking" games at a beginner's level, or if you just enjoy a more laid back version of harder hacking games.

It may be worth waiting for a sale on this one, but it isn't actually bad.

Allegedly inspired by real life privacy laws being passed in England, Mainlining is a government hacking game where you play as a member of the mysterious agency MI7, aka the "Lions". It's okay though, you're the lightly comedy kind of oppressive government. You've even got an agent who exists entirely to be a walking Twin Peaks reference. Ha ha.

You're allowed via the "BLU Pill Act" to hack into any PC you want, but you can only arrest people if you can produce evidence towards one of three charges: Selling illegal items (5 years), Theft of data or physical items (10 years), or the most heinous, life-destroying crime of all... Unlicensed Software Development (25 years).

The anti-government activist group THORNS however is working on counter-hacking the hackers. Can you capture them before...

...well, nothing actually really happens, because here's the thing: Mainlining is way less a hacking game and more of a traditional point and click adventure. If there's a way to game over, I didn't find it, and I tried things like arresting random people out of the phone book a half-dozen times just to see if the newspaper articles accusing MI7 of being incompetent losers ever got more fed up. (They did not.)

So in practice the tiers of arrest serve as self-imposed difficulty levels for the most part. Poke around a little, find someone selling drugs, arrest them for 5. Or you can poke further, discover they're being framed and arrest the framer for a data violation. Or you can push further and arrest the guy who wrote the software that made it possible for the framer to do his work.

There's no branching plotlines based on who you arrest, you just kind of bomf along to the next case.

I went out of my way to investigate everything and finished this in about four hours, so it's not going to strain anybody. However, it's because I went out of my way to investigate everything that I'm not sure I can rec this one very hard.

By the end of the game the typos are out of control (including in MISSION CRITICAL places, which ought to be a showstopper right there), the plot makes less and less sense, and more and more sites are introduced that you SHOULD be able to hack but can't. You'll have a great idea about where to look next and ... oops, no, that site mentioned in an email doesn't actually exist. 

I spent a fair amount of time towards the endgame going "Oh. Well that should've worked though?" and that's never something you want people saying about your adventure game. I feel like there was a big scope in mind and they had to cut it down and cut it back for actual release.

Mainlining has a lot of cute ideas about the hacking genre, and it's not a total wash of a game. It's just flawed, and you really really have to know that going in.

Not counting the graphical bugs which there are plenty of, the game just wasn't that fun. Sometimes there were combinations of evidence that would've made perfect sense, and yet the game still requested that you do it their way. I don't know if it bugged out for me or what, but the failure screens also kept saying the same thing even though I got different things wrong on an occasion. The story transition between the WinXP and WinVista segment was also sudden and made no real sense. There's probably more little things I disliked but eh, overall I can't really recommend this.
This game is a great adventure that, while takes a short time, is really well written and a well developed game. 11/10 but want more episodes

[h1] Neutral Recommendation: Only Pick Up At A Discount [/h1]

- [b]Gameplay:[/b]  Interfacing with the game is fairly straightforward. You're using a simulation of a computer desktop. The main complaint is that you can only backspace to make changes to text in the Notepad program. You cannot edit the text freely, so if you want to make a change to something at the top of the file, you'd have to erase everything and start over. Luckily, you'll find that program is mostly useless.

The lame thing is that, for most cases, you can only turn in one-piece of evidence linking the person to the crime, although there may be several in reality. Also, you have to pick the right location for the person, so even if you have the evidence correct, if you don't choose the right location, it somehow ends up as a False Arrest. It doesn't really make any sense that you could have sufficient evidence, but a person is [i][b]Falsely Accused[/b][/i] because they were in a different location than you originally thought they were (i.e. at work instead of at home.) That's just dumb...

- [b]Plot/Story:[/b]  This is also fairly straightforward and not very awe-inspiring. You're working for a Big Brother goverment agency that was hacked and it's your job to bring down the Cyber Terrorists in fine fashion. The story is mostly told through Emails and Documents you find while hacking systems. It is honestly pretty forgettable, and is not very long.

- [b]Graphics:[/b]  This is a very minimalist retro-style game. The text takes a bit to get used to reading, in its pixelated format. There are no actual graphics options for tuning the look of the game.

- [b]Music:[/b]  The soundtrack is actually decent for this type of game. It's nothing to shake a stick at, but was mostly just chill music to give a spy-ish undertone to the game.

- [b]Overall:[/b]  I give the game a [b]6.5/10[/b]. It's fairly short, and was kind of interesting to play through, but it is an utterly forgettable experience that will leave you wanting to play something similar, but with much better design. Also... you will come to hate the chime sound every time you get a new chat or email.

While I enjoyed my first 3 hours of the game, I ran into a bug that first appeared to inhibit my progress in the game. While the bug seemed like a significant oversight in the development process, one bug is understandable and after doing an online search I determined that you could still complete the mission while the bug was being worked on.
What made Mainlining an utterly frustrating experience for me was receiving specific instruction in the game that were not correct. There is one mission in particular where your partner says you must provide a legal document to prove that someone had a name change. I did this and failed the mission.
On top of that (same mission), the suspect lived in one area, but had expressed that he was going to move back home with his parents in an email. When I tried arresting the subject in the area where his parents live, I failed the mission and was met with a message that said attempting to make an arrest in that area failed to produce a suspect. I then tried to make an arrest where the suspect stated he lived. I was met with another message that I failed the mission, but that the area I made the arrest produced the suspect. I thought to myself, okay, I now know this person lives in this area, but I must have the wrong evidence. This was a little frustrating already given that my AI partner said I had to provide legal evidence of a name change and that's the evidence I was presenting.
I then tried evidence after evidence, clicking through documents and trying them out in my arrest attempt with the same suspect in the area where he said he lived. I kept receiving fail messages. I thought, okay, maybe I completely missed a small detail and have the wrong suspect.
I reviewed each document in the mission and determined that either I'm totally missing something or I'm experiencing a serious progress bug. I finally quit the game and go online to find out the answer (,which can be a frustrating thing to have to do for a video game). I find out that I had the correct suspect and had the correct evidence at one point in my many attempts, but the location I was attempting the arrest in was incorrect and the suspect was actually in the area where his parents live.
I was incredibly frustrated with this given that the game not only was telling me in my failed attempts that searching for the suspect in the area where his parents live fails to produce a suspect, but also that the 'correct' evidence to produce was not what your AI partner told you to provide and was not even in the top 3 pieces of evidence that seemed like the logical choice. This poor communication in the instruction, misinformation, and seemingly inflexible choice to go about the arrest made for an all-around frustrating experience in an otherwise good game (minus the aforementioned bug I came across).
Given Steam's policy of not being able to play games after 2 hours of play, I was unable to refund the game. I certainly understand having such a policy in place and I'm not blaming the developers for this complaint, but it only adds frustration when you run into so many issues in a game that inhibit progress and point to poor design and oversight after only 3 hours of play. I love the aesthetic, premise, and mechanics of Mainlining, but my frustration with the game (and Steam) has lead me not to continue playing this game.
